 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

   

 Supreme Court Appeal Numbers: S:AP:IE:2025:000056 

 Court of Appeal Record No.: 2024/71 

 High Court Record No.: 2023/2R 

   

 [2026] IESC 4 

   

   

 Dunne J. 

 O'Malley J. 

 Murray J. 

 Collins J. 

 Donnelly J. 

   

   

   

 BETWEEN/ 

   

 SEAN FLAHERTY 

   

                                                                         APPELLANT 

  AND  

   

 THE REVENUE COMMISSIONERS 

   

 RESPONDENT 

 

 JUDGEMENT of Mr. Justice Brian Murray delivered this 28 th day of January 2026 

 1.       On 21 October 2015 the appellant, Mr. Flaherty, executed a Memorandum of Agreement (' the Agreement ') for the sale to Antarctic Polyvalent Fishing Company Limited ( 'the purchaser' ) of a fishing vessel, Glór na dTonn . The equipment on the boat, all spare parts in the possession of Mr. Flaherty and what was termed ' the Capacity of the Vessel' were to be transferred to the purchaser as part of the Agreement. The questions raised in this appeal by way of Case Stated from a determination of the Tax Appeal Commission ( 'TAC' ) are directed to the point in time at which the appellant thus disposed of the vessel for the purposes of s. 542 of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 ('TCA'). If the disposal took place after 1 January 2016, the appellant is entitled pursuant to s. 597AA TCA to claim ' revised entrepreneur relief' on the disposal. The effect of that relief (which arises where a taxpayer has disposed of their business) is that a taxpayer is entitled to avail of it will pay Capital Gains Tax (' CGT ') at a reduced rate of 20% on the first 1,000,000 of a chargeable gain on the sale. If the disposal took place in 2015 - when the Agreement was entered into - the appellant is not entitled to that relief and must pay the tax at the full rate of 33% on all of his gains. 

   

 2.       In disputing that the disposal took place when the Agreement was entered into, the appellant says that it was subject to three conditions: the execution of a Bill of Sale, the application for and grant to the purchaser of a sea fishing licence in respect of the vessel, and the application for and issuing of a certificate of registration. Because, he contended, each of these requirements could be frustrated at any stage by various third parties, he said that the Agreement was a conditional contract. The effect of s. 542(1)(b) TCA is that where a contract is conditional, the time at which a disposal is made shall be the time at which the condition is satisfied. Because the second and third of these putative conditions were not satisfied until 11 January 2016, it was only then - he says - that a ' disposal' took place. Therefore, the appellant argues, he is entitled to claim ' revised entrepreneur relief' on the disposal (pursuant to s. 597AA TCA) 

   

 3.       The Appeal Commissioner (' the Commissioner ') disagreed, finding that the Agreement did not contain any express or implied conditions regarding the sale of the vessel, that in consequence, the date of disposal was 21 October 2015 and, accordingly, that the appellant's claim for revised entrepreneur relief should be refused. The appellant then filed a request for a Case Stated in accordance with s. 949AP TCA, and the Commissioner - having received submissions from the parties - framed six questions for the High Court. These questions were directed, one way or another, to whether the Commissioner erred in this conclusion. 

   

 4.       The High Court ( [2023] IEHC 764 ) (Nolan J) and the Court of Appeal ( [2025] IECA 67 ) (Whelan J: Faherty and Meenan JJ. concurring), having broadly agreed with the Commissioner, this Court granted leave to appeal against the decision of the Court of Appeal ([2025] IESCDET 82). The construction of s. 542(1) TCA, the Court said, was a matter of general public importance, and the form of contract used in the case might widely engage tax planning. 

   

 ***** 

   

 5.       In the course of his decision, the Commissioner outlined the background, referring to a number of documents to which I will turn later. While not recorded as findings of fact by the Commissioner, his account is common case. Thus, the appellant, a fisherman from Rossaveal, County Galway, was the beneficial owner of the fishing vessel Glór na dTonn with a related capacity-tonnage. The appellant was the holder of a sea fishing licence granted in relation to the vessel, this being a legal pre-requisite to using it for the purposes of sea fishing. On 21 October 2015, the appellant entered into the Agreement to which I have earlier referred. The Agreement is short, and its text is reproduced in full as an Appendix to this judgment. The relevant provisions appear as follows: 

   

 (i)                  The vendor agreed to sell and Antarctic Polyvalent Fishing Company Ltd. (' the purchaser ') agreed to purchase Glór na dTonn ( 'the vessel' ), the equipment thereon, spare parts in the ownership of the vendor and the ' Capacity ' thereof ' with all Plans and Certificates relating to the Vessel in the Vendor's possession or under its control, at the date of delivery of the Vessel.' The consideration was 5,000,000 (the Recitals and clause 1.1). This first clause of the Agreement was expressed to be ' [s]ubject to the provisions of this agreement ...' . 

   

 (ii)               Upon signing of the Agreement, the purchaser was to pay a 10% deposit in the amount of 500,000 ' to be held by Maya O'Donnell solicitors, pending completion of this Agreement' (clause 2.1). 

   

 (iii)             ' On completion' the purchaser would pay the balance of 4,500,000 ' in exchange for the completion documentation' identified in the Second Schedule of the Agreement (clause 2.2). 

   

 (iv)              The total amount of the consideration would be held in trust pending receipt by the purchaser of a validly executed Bill of Sale by the vendor transferring ownership of the vessel and ' Capacity Assignment ', together with the equipment, spare parts, plans, certificates and all documents relating to the vessel set out in the Second Schedule, on completion. Moreover, on completion the vendor would hand to the purchaser the keys and would maintain the insurance over the vessel until the completion date (clauses 2.3, 2.4 and 2.5). 

   

 (v)                Both clause 2.3 and clause 3.1 made clear that completion would take place following receipt by the vendor of the balance of the purchase monies, and receipt by the purchaser's solicitor of the documentation specified in the Second Schedule to the Agreement, and that on completion the vendor would deliver the vessel to the purchaser at Killybegs. The date for completion was left blank, save that it was to occur in 2015. The completion clause contained a proviso ' subject to the provisions in Clause 1.2 hereof' . The Agreement did not contain a clause 1.2. 

   

 (vi)              Clause 6 provided that if the vessel was lost before completion, the Agreement would become null and void, and the deposit would be returned. If damage was caused which would cost more than 10,000 to correct, the purchase price would be reduced while if damage was caused that would cost more than 50,000 to correct, the purchaser was at liberty to rescind the contract in which event the deposit would be returned. 

   

 (vii)           Clause 8 provided that if the vendor failed to execute a legal transfer or to deliver the vessel within the time specified in clause 3, the purchaser would have the right to cancel the contract, in which case the deposit would be returned with interest at the rate of 2% per annum. There was no time specified in clause 3. 

   

 (viii)         The First Schedule to the Agreement included details of the vessel, including its gross tonnage (230 GT). The Second Schedule identified the documents to be delivered on completion. These included a ' Bill of Sale'. The last item specified on the Second Schedule is described as ' Confirmation of Fishing Entitlements' . 

   

 6.       The appellant's case as to conditionality hinged on these latter four words and the three references in the Agreement to ' Capacity' (the Recital, clause 1.1 and clause 2.3). His argument was that the fishing entitlements referred to here included registration of the boat and the sea-fishing licence, and that the ' capacity' of the vessel (which he also equated to an entitlement to fish) could not be assigned by the vendor to the purchaser, instead being surrendered, extinguished and re-issued by the authorities. Unless and until the ' Confirmation of Fishing Entitlements' to which reference is made here and - if different - the ' capacity' was delivered to the purchaser, he contended, there was no binding legal obligation on the purchaser part to accept or pay for, the vessel. Therefore, he argued, the contract was ' conditional' within the meaning of s. 542(1)(b) TCA. 

   

 7.       Section 542(1) TCA provides as follows: 

   

 '542.  (1)(a) Subject to paragraph (b) and subsection (2), for the purposes of the Capital Gains Tax Act, where an asset is disposed of and acquired under a contract, the time at which the disposal and acquisition is made shall be the time at which the contract is made (and not, if different, the time at which the asset is conveyed or transferred). 

   

 (b) Where the contract is conditional (and in particular where it is conditional on the exercise of an option), the time at which the disposal and acquisition is made shall be the time at which the condition is satisfied.' 

   

 ***** 

   

 8.       To understand both the appellant's argument, and indeed more generally the manner in which the Agreement fell to be completed, it is necessary to touch on the extensive regulatory framework governing the ownership and use of sea fishing vessels in the State. The following eight features of that legislative context are relevant [1] : 

   

 (i)                  Generally, a sea-fishing boat may not be used for sea-fishing save under and in accordance with a sea-fishing boat licence granted in relation to the boat (s. 97 Sea-Fisheries and Maritime Jurisdiction Act 2006 ( 'the 2006 Act' ), inserting an amended s. 4 of the Fisheries (Amendment) Act 2003) ( 'the 2003 Act' )). The licence is granted by the Registrar General of Fishing Boats (' the licensing authority' ) (s. 3 of the 2003 Act). An application for a licence must be made by or on behalf of the owner of the vessel (s. 4(3)(b)(iii)). The application must specify the tonnage and engine capacity of the boat, whether the vessel is presently on the Irish Sea Fishing Boat Register and, if so, whether the vessel has been acquired ' complete with capacity' or if not, the boats ' from which it is proposed that capacity will be withdrawn.' The licence is granted to a named person, and once that person ceases to be the owner of the boat, the licence ceases to have effect and must be delivered to the licensing authority (s. 4(12)(a)). Any new sea fishing boat licence will require an application by or on behalf of the new owner. Thus, in order to obtain a new sea fishing boat licence, ownership of the vessel must be transferred to the purchaser prior to their application for that licence. 

   

 (ii)               Section 75(1) of the 2006 Act also requires that every Irish sea-fishing boat shall be entered on the Register of Fishing Boats. It is an offence not to do so (s. 75(6)). A sea fishing boat shall not be entered in that Register unless at the time of entry there is in relation to the boat a sea fishing boat licence which is either in force, or if not so in force is to come into force on the boat being so registered (s. 75(3)(a)). This Register is maintained by the Registrar General of Fishing Boats. 

   

 (iii)             The application for registration on the Register of Fishing Boats must be made by the owner of the fishing boat (Merchant Shipping (Registry, Lettering and Numbering of Fishing Boats) Regulations 2005, SI 261/2005: Regulation 8(1) [2] ) ( 'S.I. 261/2005' ). Where ownership of a registered fishing boat changes, the existing and new owners are obliged to notify the change and have the Register updated to reflect the new owner ( id. Regulation 15(2)). Implementing the provisions of s. 75(3)(a) of the 2006 Act, the boat can only be so registered where the Registrar is satisfied that the appellant has been granted a sea fishing boat licence under s.4 of the 2003 Act which would become operative on or after the registration of the boat on the Register of Fishing Boats ( id. Regulation 8(4)(b)). Applications for registration are made through the agency of local registrars ( id. Regulation 8(2)). Thus, in order to obtain a certificate of registration also, a purchaser must first have acquired ownership of the vessel. 

   

 (iv)              The Mercantile Marine Act 1955 ( 'the 1955 Act' ) defines ' ship ' in terms that include ' every description of vessel used in navigation not propelled by oars' ( s. 2 of the 1955 Act). It mandates that certain ships (those in excess of fifteen net register tons) be registered in accordance with the Act (s. 18(2)(a)) and then provides that a ship so registered, when disposed of to a qualified person, ' shall be transferred by bill of sale' (s. 43(1)). 

   

 (v)                Regulation 11(1) of S.I. 261/2005 as promulgated, provided that the tonnage to be recorded in the Register in relation to a fishing boat shall be its tonnage as determined in accordance with Council Regulation (EEC) No. 2930/86 of 22 September 1986, together with subsequent amending Regulations and Decisions. These EU provisions have since been replaced by Regulation (EU) 2017/1130 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 June 2017 defining the characteristics for fishing vessels. That Regulation now defines, inter alia, tonnage (Article 4) and engine power (Article 5). Those provisions are expressly adopted in the Irish penalty-points regime as the basis for fishing capacity ( id. Regulation 3(1) of S.I. 318/2020). Regulation (EU) 2017/1130 also prescribes the methodology for the calculation of the tonnage and engine power of vessels. 

   

 (vi)              Under Articles 22 and 23 of Regulation (EU) 1380/2013 of 11 December 2013 on the Common Fisheries Policy, each Member State must stay below a fixed capacity ceiling - one in GT and one in kW - and apply an ' entry/exist scheme' whereby any new capacity entering the fleet must be balanced by prior withdrawal of at least the same GT and the same kW (see Articles 22(1) and 23(1)) of Regulation (EU) 1380/2013) 

   

 (vii)           As already noted, in S.I. 318/2020, ' fishing capacity' in relation to an Irish sea-fishing boat is defined as meaning its tonnage and engine power within the meaning of this Regulation (Regulation 3(1) of S.I. 318/2020). This reflects well established usage in EU legal provisions: Article 4(24) of EU Regulation 1380/2013 defines capacity in this way, and Article 38(1) of EU Council Regulation No. 1224/2009 provides: 

   

   

 ' Member States shall be responsible for carrying out the necessary checks in order to ensure that the total capacity corresponding to the fishing licences issued by a Member State, in GT and in kW, shall at any moment not be higher than the maximum capacity levels for that Member State ...' 

   

 (viii)         Finally, the regulations recognise 'off register/deregister' capacity as fishing capacity that is not for the time being assigned to an Irish sea fishing boat (that is before a licence for the vessel has been granted by the Licensing Authority) (Regulation 10(4) and (5) of SI 318/2020). 

   

 9.       It follows that capacity (as thus defined in the EU provisions to which I have referred) is a privately held and traded asset, and the maintenance of capacity is relevant to the licensing and registration of Irish sea fishing boats due to the requirements of EU law intended to enable a balance between fishing capacity and the maintenance of fish stocks. It is the system of fishing vessel licensing that controls the size and fishing capacity (tonnage and power) of the fleets in the Member States for the purposes of the EU scheme for fishing fleet management (see Long, Marine Resource Law in Ireland (Thomson Round Hall Dublin 2007) ( 'Long' ) at para. [4-97]). Generally, entries and exits from the fishing fleet must be managed so that the entry of new capacity into any segment of the fleet must be compensated by the previous withdrawal of at least the same amount of capacity from that same segment of the fleet (see, Long , at para. [4-97]). Thus, the Court was told, where an application is made to remove a vessel from the Sea Fishing Boat Register, the tonnage and engine capacity must be identified, and if these are being assigned, the assignee specified. Similarly, where an application is made for a Sea Fishing Boat licence, the appellant must specify the tonnage and engine capacity of the vessel if previously on the Register, and if not, the vessels from which it is proposed that that capacity will be withdrawn. Thus understood, capacity is not in itself a form of free-standing fishing entitlement: rather it only becomes part of an entitlement when (a) it is tied to a specific vessel in the fleet register and (b) that vessel holds a valid fishing licence.  And, critically for the purposes of this case, in order to obtain a sea-fishing licence and a certificate of registration in respect of a vessel ownership of which has changed, the purchaser must actually have ownership vested in him. 

   

 ***** 

   

 10.   The transfer of Glór na dTonn proceeded in accordance with the scheme envisaged by these provisions. On 1 December 2015, the Licensing Authority for Sea Fishing Boats (an official in the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine) wrote to the appellant in reference to an application he had obviously made to remove Glór na dTonn from the Fishing Boat Register. She said that consideration could not be given to removing the vessel from the Fishing Boat Register until three things were done: (a) either an outstanding mortgage was paid, or the mortgagee consented, (b) certain harbour dues were paid, and (c) an outstanding grant to Bord Iascaigh Mhara was discharged. 

   

 11.   The first payment of the monies due under the Agreement was made by the purchaser on 17 December 2015 (in the amount of 65,000). A Bill of Sale in relation to the sale of the vessel was signed and dated by the appellant on 21 December 2015. That document recorded the horsepower of the engines (447 kW [3] ) and the tonnage of the vessel (230 gross and 69 registered). Before the Commissioner, it was accepted by the appellant that the vessel itself was transferred to the purchaser on that date (the Bill of Sale acknowledged that the transfer had taken place, and indeed that the sum of 5,000,000 had been paid pursuant to the Agreement). A Declaration of Ownership dated 22 December 2015 records Eamonn McHugh, director, as confirming that Antarctic Polyvalent Fishing Company Ltd. is ' entitled to be registered as owner of 64 ... shares in [Glór na d'Tonn]' and that ' no other person or body of persons other than such persons or bodies of persons ... is entitled, as owner, to any interest whatsoever, either legal or beneficial, in the said Ship or in any share therein.' The respondent says that these documents, together with others, were sent to the Register of Shipping, Port of Galway, by Art Kavanagh, Marine Finance Consultant, on 22 December 2015 as part of a package of material accompanying an application to register Glór na dTonn. Counsel for the appellant is recorded in the Commissioner's decision as having submitted that the vessel had to be transferred into the purchaser's name, as this was necessary in order to allow the purchaser request that the associated licence and tonnage be transferred to them in their capacity as new owners of the vessel. The declaration by the purchaser that he was the owner of the vessel was, counsel for the appellant said, ' an interim statement' . 

   

 12.   On 7 January 2016, the Licensing Authority for Sea Fishing Boats e-mailed Mr. Kavanagh in the following terms: 

   

 ' The vessel 'Glór na D'Tonn' G454 has been deregistered and capacity has been assigned to Antarctic Polyvalent Fishing Co Ltd as per capacity assignment note. Shane Crowley is in the process of completing the non-operative licence. Once it is in order he will email it directly to Antarctic Polyvalent Fishing Co Ltd and to Mary Martyn, Registrar of Shipping in Galway.' (emphasis added) 

   

 13.   It might be observed that no ' capacity assignment note' appears in the papers, and indeed that counsel for the appellant was uncertain as to whether such a note had ever been executed. [4] By letter addressed to the purchaser and dated 11 January 2016, the Department of Agriculture Food and the Marine confirmed that the Licensing Authority had decided to grant a non-operative licence to the purchaser pursuant to s. 4 of the 2003 Act (as inserted by s. 97 of the 2006 Act). This licence was valid only for the purposes of registration and for a period of three months from the date of its issue, and it recorded that while the licence did not permit the boat to which it referred to engage in commercial sea fishing, it allowed the purchaser to re-register the vessel as a sea fishing boat. This non-operative licence thus enabled the purchaser to comply with the requirement imposed by s. 75(3)(a) of the 2006 Act that there be a sea-fishing licence in force in relation to the vessel before it is registered. 

   

 14.   The letter granting the non-operative licence stated that a sea-fishing licence for the purposes of fishing would be issued only when the boat was entered in the Fishing Boat Register in the purchaser's name. Upon being registered, the operative sea-fishing licence could then issue recording its registration. It appears that there is no specific legislative authority for the issue of such an ' non-operative licence' but (according to the letter of 11 January 2016) it was issued pursuant to a Departmental Policy Directive, for the purposes of enabling the entry of the boat on the Fishing Boat Register. The letter recorded ' the capacity from the MVF 'Glór na dTonn' G454 must be re-introduced on to the Sea Fishing Boat Register by 6 th January 2018' . 

   

 15.   A Certificate of Registration of an Irish Fishing Vessel then issued in respect of the vessel on 11 January 2016. On the same date, an operative Sea Fishing Boat Licence issued to the purchaser in respect of the vessel. Subsequent payments were then made by the purchaser on foot of the Agreement on 19 January 2016 (4,930,000) and 10 February 2016 (5,000). 

   

 16.   Having submitted his CGT computation on the basis that the disposal took place in the 2016 tax year, the appellant claimed revised entrepreneur relief under s. 597AA TCA. The respondent having raised a series of queries on this, and various correspondence being thereafter exchanged between the parties, a Notice of Assessment to CGT eventually issued on 27 April 2018 in the sum of 130,000, this being the quantum of the disputed relief. That was then appealed to the TAC. 

   

 17.   The Commissioner in his Determination, as well as finding that the Agreement had been entered into on 21 October 2015, that the appellant submitted his CGT computation to the respondent which recorded the date of disposal as occurring in the 2016 tax year, and that a dispute had arisen between the appellant and the respondent as to whether the sale occurred in the 2015 or 2016 tax year, found (at para. 38 of the Commissioner's Determination and para. 8 of the Case Stated): 

   

 (i)                  That the vessel and the related capacity/tonnage were required to be disposed of together for the sale to be effective. 

   

 (ii)               That a number of steps were required to be undertaken to ensure that the vessel, licence and fishing rights were transferred to the purchaser. 

   

 (iii)             That if those steps were not fulfilled, ' it is likely that the Memorandum entered into between the parties would have become frustrated.' 

   

 ***** 

   

 18.   The hearing before the Commissioner proceeded without oral evidence. The Commissioner in his decision reduced the dispute to (a) whether the Agreement was conditional upon various licences being obtained and/or (b) whether a term should be implied into the agreement to the effect that it was so conditional. In contending that such a term should be implied, the appellant invoked what the Commissioner described as ' the doctrine of business efficacy'. 

   

 19.   The Commissioner agreed with the respondent's submissions that the requirements identified in Schedule 2 of the Agreement 'were procedural rather than conditional in nature and given this position does not find that the wording of the Memorandum gives rise to any express conditions.' (para. 44). It was emphasised that the Memorandum of Agreement did not contain any 'subject to' or similar 'contingent conditions' (para 46). It was stressed again that 'the language used in the Memorandum and the actions of the parties up to the closure of the sale reinforce the Commissioner's belief that the Memorandum does not contain any express conditions.' (para. 46). While agreeing that completion of the agreement could not have occurred until all of the relevant documentation was furnished by the appellant to the purchaser and the relevant statutory provisions were complied with, the Commissioner observed that '... had the agreement not completed for one reason or another, there would have been no disposal for CGT purposes and the date of disposal would not be in issue.' (para. 45). Insofar as it had been contended that the sale of the appellant's vessel could be likened to that of a property sold subject to planning permission, the Commissioner observed that the Agreement did not contain any ' subject to' or similar contingent conditions (para. 46). He declined to imply a term of the kind contended for by the appellant, observing that the only tangible effect of implying such a term would have been that the appellant would be liable to pay less CGT and this, he said, did not satisfy the ' business efficacy' test (para. 49). The Commissioner concluded at para. 50 of its Determination that the Memorandum of 21 October 2015 'did not contain any express or implied conditions regarding the sale and as such that the relevant date of the disposal is 21st October 2015. As this finding places the disposal into the 2015 tax year it follows that entrepreneur's relief must be denied to the Appellant and the assessment in the sum of 130,000 is upheld.' 

   

 20.   A request to state a case to the High Court having then been made, and the parties having exchanged submissions as regards the content of that Case Stated, the Commissioner framed the following questions for the High Court on 16 December 2022: 

   

 1.                   Did the Commissioner err in his interpretation that the Memorandum of Agreement did not contain any express or implied conditions regarding the sale? 

   

 2.                   Did the Commissioner err at para. 38.5 of his Determination in stating that one of the steps required to be taken under the Memorandum of Agreement was to 'ensure licence and fishing rights were transferred to the purchaser' rather than 'be surrendered by the vendor and the purchaser given equivalent fishing rights'? If so, does this have any impact on the Memorandum being conditional in nature? 

   

 3.                   Did the Commissioner err in his Determination in holding that matters affecting the sale requiring third-party consent did not amount to express or implied conditional terms of the Memorandum? 

   

 4.                   Did the Commissioner err in determining that, if the procedural steps were not fulfilled, this would have caused the Memorandum to become frustrated? 

   

 5.                   Did the Commissioner err in determining that the doctrine of business efficacy was not applicable in the instant circumstances? 

   

 6.                   Did the Commissioner err in his interpretation that the Memorandum entered into between the appellant and the purchaser on 21 October 2015 was not a conditional contract? 

   

 ***** 

   

 21.   Nolan J. decided that all but Question 2 should be answered in the negative (para. 63). Question 2 was whether the Commissioner erred in stating that one of the steps required to be taken under the Agreement was to ' ensure licence and fishing rights were transferred to the purchaser' rather than ' be surrendered by the vendor and the purchaser given an equivalent fishing rights' . The actual procedure, Nolan J. said, was the latter not the former (para. 63). However, he decided, this did not have any impact on the Agreement being conditional in nature. Thus, the essential conclusions reached by the Commissioner were upheld. 

   

 22.   In his judgment, Nolan J. rejected the appellant's submission that the sale of the vessel was similar to that of a property sold 'subject to planning permission' (para. 56). Nolan J. noted the absence of conditional words in the agreement: 'Nowhere does the agreement say that the sale is subject to the obtaining of any of the documents set out in the schedule.' He considered that '[t]he issue as to when the contract became enforceable may well be a matter for the parties to the contract, but it is not an issue which the Commissioner should take into consideration in interpreting the tax code' (para. 56). Nolan J. emphasised that the contract provided that the balance of the purchase price would be paid in exchange for the completion documentation, and did not provide that the contract was conditional upon receiving the completion documentation. If these were never received, he said, there would be no contract and therefore there would be no disposal and accordingly no CGT liability (para. 58) 

   

 23.   Having considered s. 542 TCA 1997, Nolan J. concluded that the section made a clear distinction between a conditional requirement and an act required to be done before an asset is conveyed or transferred. He cited the decision of Baker J. in Murphy v. O'Toole & Sons Ltd. & Anor. [2014] IEHC 486 as authority for the proposition that for a contract to be conditional, the condition must be expressed between the parties in clear words (para. 60). Nolan J. was of the view that the requirements as regards the furnishing of documentation and other steps were ' procedural and not conditional' and held that the Commissioner was correct in concluding that the Memorandum of Agreement did not contain any express/implied conditions regarding the sale. There were, he emphasised, no conditional words used in the Agreement. Nowhere, he concluded, did it say that the sale was subject to the obtaining of any of the documents set out in the schedule. Furthermore, Nolan J. held that the Commissioner was correct in determining that matters affecting the sale requiring third-party consent did not amount to express or implied conditional terms and that even if the procedural steps (such as, obtaining the licence from the Fishing Licence Authority) were not fulfilled, this would have caused the Agreement to be frustrated. He attached particular importance to the contents of the Bill of Sale which, he said, pointed to the transaction having been concluded. Finally, Nolan J. determined that the Commissioner was correct in holding that what was termed ' the doctrine of business efficacy' was not applicable to the case. 

   

 ***** 

   

 24.   The Court of Appeal agreed. Its reasons were given in a detailed and comprehensive judgment delivered by Whelan J. Whelan J. began her analysis by observing the distinction between promissory and contingent contracts, and the further distinction within the latter category of agreement between those subject to conditions precedent, and those subject to conditions subsequent (para. 41). A condition precedent, she explained, is a fact that is a necessary perquisite for the creation of a binding contract, while a condition subsequent is one that will determine the contract on the occurrence of the specified event. A contingent contract, she later explained, is one where the obligation of the parties pursuant to its terms are contingent on some future event, while a promissory contract arises where one party to the transaction agrees to perform an obligation (as illustrated in Eastham v. Leigh London and Provincial Properties Ltd. [1971] Ch. 871) (' Eastham' ) (at para. 84). The fact, she said, that a contract is subject to promissory conditions precedent to completion does not make it conditional in the sense of being subject to contingent conditions: a promissory agreement is binding from the outset. Likewise, a condition pursuant to which the contract might come to an end on the failure by a party to perform obligations under a contractual term does not render it subject to a contingent condition subsequent. Rather it is a promissory condition subsequent. Where, Whelan J. said, the requirement to obtain planning permission is merely a matter of conveyance because the obligation to sell is already binding, then the contract will be treated as unconditional. Like principles applied where an aspect of the transaction involves an input by a third party, as in this case. 

   

 25.   Noting that a condition precedent to completion does not prevent a binding contract from coming into existence ab initio (and citing in that connection the decision in Property and Bloodstock Limited v. Emerton [1968] 1 Ch 94 and Perri v. Coolangatta Investments Property Ltd. (1982) 149 CLR 537 ( 'Perri' )) it was, Whelan J. said, only conditions precedent (she later described these as ' contingent conditions precedent ') that are captured by s. 542(1)(b) (citing Eastham ) and Lyon (Inspector of Taxes) v. Pettigrew ( 'Lyon' ) and Hatt v. Newman (Inspector of Taxes) ( 'Hatt' ) (at para. 66). The ' contingent conditions precedent' referred to in s. 542(1)(b), Whelan J. explained, arose where the contract is subject to a contingency going beyond express obligations assumed by the parties pursuant to the contract such as a condition precedent to performance, and where it was subject instead to a condition precedent to its formation (para. 70). In that situation, there is no legally binding contract until such time as the condition precedent has been satisfied. Conditions subsequent, she explained, do not render a contract ' conditional' for the purposes of s. 542(1)(b) TCA. She cited examples of such contracts from Wylie and Woods ' Irish Conveyancing Law'  conditions that have to be fulfilled before an obligation to complete arises such as conditions subject to the purchaser obtaining a mortgage loan, planning permission for specified development or the consent of the landlord to the assignment of a lease.  32.   Noting that there is no issue between the parties arising from the findings of fact of the Commissioner and that, accordingly, the questions in this appeal are solely matters of legal interpretation, it is convenient to separate out three issues that arise - (a) the meaning of the phrase ' [w]here the contract is conditional' as it appears in s. 542(1)(b) TCA, (b) whether the express terms of the Agreement render same ' conditional' thus interpreted, and - if the answer to (b) is negative - (c) whether it is possible or appropriate to imply a term into the Agreement that will render it so conditional. 

   

 33.   What is now s. 542(1)(b) first appeared on the statute book in the form of s. 10(1)(b) of the Capital Gains Tax Act 1975. That legislation introduced the first tax on capital gains in Ireland. The provision has remained in, essentially, the same form since. It mirrored the provisions of the United Kingdom Finance Act 1971, Schedule 10, para. 10(2). It is necessary to an understanding of the earlier English cases addressing the language used in these sections to observe that the latter provision, in turn, reflected the terms of s. 12(2) of the Finance Act 1962 ( 'the 1962 Act' ), which introduced income tax on short term gains. That tax applied to disposals which occurred within a defined period of acquisition. It was, therefore, necessary for the legislation to specify with precision exactly when both an acquisition, and a disposal, took place for the purposes of the charge to tax: the earlier English cases are notable insofar as - for this reason - the revenue authorities were generally concerned to pitch an acquisition as having occurred at the later of any possible date, and the disposal at the earliest. 

   

 34.   Whatever the object in its original iteration (and there was never any equivalent in Ireland of such a short-term gains tax), the purpose of the provision now is, obviously, to define the point in time at which a disposal (or for that matter, and where relevant, an acquisition) takes place for the purposes of Capital Gains Tax. It does so in a context in which, but for the section, it might be said that in at least some situations, the date of disposal of the asset is the point at which the owner divests themselves of all legal or beneficial interest in it. Indeed, the language of the provision itself assumes that proposition (' and not ... the time at which the asset is conveyed or transferred ...' ). Given that the date of disposal of an asset may determine the rate of Capital Gains Tax payable, or the availability of allowances or rate of allowances, or whether certain losses can be set against gains, it is equally obvious that the Oireachtas needed to specify a clear point at which the tax would attach to a disposal. The date of disposal provided for, accordingly, is a deemed date of disposal, not an actual one, and it is deemed solely ' for the purposes of the Capital Gains Tax Acts' (s. 541(1)(c) TCA). Moreover, what is deemed is a date, not a disposal (see, in this regard, the judgment of Lord Hoffmann in Jerome v. Kelly [2004] UKHL 25 , [2004] 1 WLR 1409 ( 'Jerome' ) at para. 11). The disposal and acquisition may well, as a matter of law, be found to involve actions that occur after the deemed date, notably where it is determined (as in Jerome ) that it actually occurs on completion of the relevant contract. Section 542 TCA does not dictate that these cease to constitute the disposal, merely that that event is deemed to have occurred at an earlier date: '[i]t [was intended to] deal only with the question of fixing the time of disposal and not with the substantive liability to tax' ( Underwood v. Revenue and Customs Commissioners [2008] EWCA Civ 1423 per Collins LJ at para. 4 in consideration of the United Kingdom's legislative equivalent s. 28(1) of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992). 

   

 35.    And, in this regard, it will be noted that a contract can ' be made' for the disposal of an asset, but without the asset actually being disposed of. For any one of a number of reasons, the contract may never complete and in these situations no liability for Capital Gains Tax will arise because there has been no ' disposal' . But if it does complete and there has, thus, been a disposal, the deemed date of disposal relates back to the date of contract, not of completion. The provision, as counsel for the respondent put it, ' looks back' to a date of disposal, but only after a disposal has actually occurred. 

   

 36.   The trigger for the section is disposal and acquisition ' under' a contract. This is broad language. It directs attention to the source of the obligation which was performed by the transfer of the assets which constituted the relevant disposal ( Chan v. Cresdon Property Ltd. (1989) 168 CLR 242, 249). There may be situations in which it is arguable that disposals that arise only because of a contract but which are merely enabled rather than directly triggered by that contract, might be captured. This is particularly the case in relation to the grant of an option. A and B may enter into a contract that entitles A to acquire an asset from B for a particular price at a particular time or on the occurrence of a specified event. A may never exercise the option, whether because he chooses not to, or because the event never occurs. But if and when the option is exercised, the asset is arguably acquired ' under' the original option contract even though the reality is that the event that enables the acquisition of the asset is the exercise of the option, not the contract that provides for that exercise. Indeed, without express qualification, s. 542(1)(a) could result in disposals being deemed to have occurred long before the actual event that enabled the transfer to take place. 

   

 37.   Section 542(1)(b) TCA expressly addresses that very situation. But the example instanced in the subsection underscores two important features of the provision. First, it is a derogation from the general rule that a disposal under a contract is deemed to have occurred on the date of the contract: the starting point is that where an asset is disposed of ' under a contract' any disposal happens on the date of the contract. Second, in this situation the ' conditional' contract is one in which the ' condition' operates to prevent legal obligations to dispose of and accept or pay for the asset from arising: the example in the text of s. 542(1)(b) TCA is that of the exercise of the option which triggers an obligation on the part of the other to sell or buy as the case may be. 

   

 ***** 

   

 38.   As the judgment of the Court of Appeal well shows, the use of the term ' conditional' in the law of contract is plagued by a proliferation of meanings. That judgment, and indeed the submissions of the parties, identify a number of authorities in which the different senses in which the term is used in that context, are explained - contingent contracts, promissory conditions, conditions precedent, conditions subsequent, contingent conditions precedent, conditions precedent to performance, conditions precedent to the formation or existence of a contract, ' resolutive' conditions and so forth. Some of these terms, according at least to some of the authorities, mean the same thing. Lewison ' The Interpretation of Contracts' (8 th edn, Sweet & Maxwell 2024) ( 'Lewison' ) at para. [16.01]) identifies six distinct meanings of the term - (i) a requirement which must be satisfied before any contract comes into existence, (ii) a requirement which must be satisfied before a party can be liable to perform his obligations under a contract, (iii) a term of the contract, (iv) an important term of the contract breach of which will amount to a repudiation of the contract, (v) a requirement which if satisfied will automatically bring the contract to an end, or (vi) a requirement which if satisfied will entitle one party to bring the contract to an end. 

   

 39.   While the cases and terminology considered by the Court of Appeal are helpful in illuminating the various situations that fall to be addressed by contractual conditions, there is no reason to believe that the Oireachtas had any one of these terms in mind when enacting the section - although clearly the situation it did have in mind is likely (at least in part) to be captured by one of these terms. The issue, however, is properly and more clearly viewed as one only of construction of the section in general, and the phrase ' contract is conditional ' as it appears in s. 542(1)(b) TCA, in particular. That issue must be resolved by reference to a now familiar refrain - the meaning of the words used in the provision having regard to its purpose and context. Because this is not a charging provision, and indeed because - depending on the circumstances - the fixing of the date of disposal may benefit as well as disadvantage the taxpayer, the strict rules of construction that sometimes play a part in the construction of tax legislation, do not arise. 

   

 40.   Viewing the term ' contract is conditional' in this way it is possible to identify two situations the Oireachtas did not intend to bring within the term. First, the ordinary mutual promises that subtend all executory contracts may be fairly described as rendering some or all of the contractual obligations in issue ' conditional'  A's obligation to transfer his car to B may arise only when B tenders 10,000, but B may still be obliged under the contract to tender the sum. Section 542(1)(b) TCA does not use the term ' conditional' in this sense. This is simply a promise conditional on performance. 

   

 41.   That reflects the conclusion reached in all of the cases. Eastham decided that a contract which required a party to construct a building on a property to the satisfaction of its owner, and which provided that upon completion of the building the owner would grant a lease of that property to him was not ' conditional' for the purposes of s. 12(2) of the 1962 Act. Russell LJ explained that ' I cannot accept that it is correct to say that because the grant of the lease was dependent upon the fulfilment by the tenant of those obligations which constituted the consideration for the grant of the lease, the contract to acquire can properly be described as a conditional contract at all. It is a contract for ... [the] grant and acceptance of a lease' (at p. 886). He continued: 

   

 'What is provided for in the contract is not a condition of the contract at all: it is simply a provision that the one party shall carry out certain works in consideration of a promise thereafter to grant a lease and that the other party, in consideration of those works being carried out, shall thereafter grant the lease.' 

   

 42.     In Lyon , one of the questions was whether a contract for the sale of a taxicab and associated licence was a conditional contract for the purposes of the provisions introduced by the United Kingdom's Finance Act 1971. The argument was that because property in the licence was not to pass until all instalments of the consideration had been paid, the agreement came within the United Kingdom's equivalent of s. 542(1)(b). The case was complicated by the fact that the licence and vehicle could not be detached from one another, but Walton J. addressed the argument on the assumption that property in neither was to pass. The decision of the Special Commissioners that the contract was conditional on payment of all the instalments was described by the Court as ' wholly unmaintainable' . He explained: 

   

 ' The words 'contract is conditional' have traditionally, I think, been used to cover really only two types of case. One is a 'subject to contract' contract, where there is clearly no contract at all anyway, and the other is where all the liabilities under the contract are conditional upon a certain event. ' 

   

 43.   The contract in that case was in no sense within the latter description: the parties assumed a series of obligations of which the transfer of property on the payment of the final instalment was but one. The relevant point lies in the distinction between contracts in which critical rights and obligations are dependent upon the occurrence of an event - which will be properly described as conditional - and those underpinned by mutual promises, some of which may themselves be categorised as ' conditions' . ' A contract is not conditional merely because it contains obligations which may be termed promissory conditions' ( Jerome v. Kelly per Lord Walker at para. 26). 

   

 44.   That being so, the test suggested by the appellant in his submissions that a contract is conditional until it becomes specifically enforceable - cannot be the correct one. The distinction, instead, is between a condition that prevents certain ' contractual obligations arising when the contract was concluded' and one that does not ( Hatt v. Newman (Inspector of Taxes) [2000] STC 113, per Parker LJ at 118). Certainly, if a contract is not specifically enforceable, this may be because an event that is a condition to liability under the contract has not occurred, but this is not the only reason a contract containing a condition might not be specifically enforceable: the party for whose benefit a wholly promissory condition was inserted may have lawfully repudiated liability or rescinded the contract. That differentiation between enforceable and unenforceable agreements may well have been a valid distinction for the purposes of the issues arising from the general law of contract considered by Geoghegan J. in O'Connor v. Coady [2004] 3 IR 271 ( 'O'Connor' ) and by Clarke J. in Hand v. Greaney [2004] IEHC 391 , but they are not readily transferable to the construction of s. 542(1)(b) TCA. If they were, then that provision would apply to any contract containing any condition. There is no reason whatsoever why the Oireachtas would have wished to derogate in this situation from the general rule posited in s. 542(1)(a) TCA. To construe the provision in this way would result in the exception swallowing the rule. 

   

 ***** 

   

 45.   The second situation which appears to me to be outside the scope of s. 542(1)(b) TCA is that referenced by Walton J. in Lyon who, instancing the ' subject to contract' cases observed that in those decisions, the effect of the condition was that there was no contract at all. While not a lot may turn on it, that cases of this kind are outside the scope of s. 542(1)(b) TCA follows from the relationship between it and s. 542(1)(a). Section 542(1)(a) is concerned, and concerned only, with a situation in which an asset is disposed of ' under a contract' . Section 542(1)(b) TCA is concerned with that same situation (' [w]here the contract ...' ). The structure of the section suggests that ' the contract' is the same contract as referred to in s. 542(1)(a) TCA ' under' which the asset is disposed or of acquired, and the language used puts beyond doubt that the provision assumes that there is a contract providing for an obligation, but that that obligation is itself conditional. If it was concerned with a relationship between two parties which assumed the form of a contract only on the happening of a specified event, s. 542(1)(b) would have been unnecessary: in that event there would be no contract until that event, and the matter would, thus, be captured by s. 542(1)(a). Section 542(1)(b) is solely concerned with a situation in which an asset is acquired or disposed of ' under' a contract, but in which there is a contract, and that contract is subject to a condition. 

   

 46.   Here, confusion has arisen from the use of the term ' condition precedent' in the general law of contract. Many of the cases and texts speak of a condition precedent to the existence of any contract. Others use the term to refer also to a condition precedent to performance of certain obligations under the contract but nonetheless assume that there is in fact a contract of some kind in place (see, for an example, Lewison, at para. [16.07] - ' [a] condition precedent is a condition which must be fulfilled to bringing about the creation of a contract or the enforceability of an obligation' (emphasis added)). That was the sense explained in the judgment of Gibbs CJ in Perri , which in turn influenced Geoghegan J. in his conclusion in O'Connor v. Coady [2004] 3 IR 271 (at para. 19) that the distinction between ' conditions precedent' and ' conditions subsequent' was not a helpful one. 

   

 47.   Whether that is so in the context of the law of contract generally, conditions precedent to the existence of any contractual obligation of any kind are outside the scope of s. 542(1)(b) TCA. This means that when the provision refers to a case in which ' the contract is conditional' it is using those words to describe something slightly different from the ' conditional contract' referred to by Geoghegan J. in O'Connor at para. 23, namely ' a contract which only comes into existence upon fulfilment of [a] condition'. There must be some contractual obligation, but the principal performance will be conditional on some event (Beale, Chitty On Contracts (36 th edn, Vol. 1 Sweet & Maxwell 2026) ( 'Chitty' ) at para. [4-198]). And in the context in which s. 542(1)(b) is to operate, that principal performance will be the disposition of an asset. There will be a contract, in other words, but no contract imposing obligations on the vendor to sell, or the purchaser to buy the asset until the event specified in the condition has occurred. 

   

 48.   That this is the situation to which the Oireachtas was directing its attention is best demonstrated by the paradigmatic example described in the section - that of the option. Where A grants to B an option to acquire an asset from A upon the happening of an identified event, there is a contract between A and B irrespective of whether the event occurs. The contract, to state the obvious, is one that obliges A to sell the asset when the event occurs. There is no contract for sale until the event happens, but there is a contract. As the decision in Perri shows, it is possible for there to be a binding contract in law, containing conditions that are ' precedent' to the performance of certain obligations provided for in the contract, and an option agreement is a classic example of this. That is the situation with which s. 542(1)(b) TCA is concerned: to that extent counsel for the appellant is correct when he says that the provision is not addressed to a stipulation which prevents any contract from arising. That circumstance falls to be regulated by s. 542(1)(a) TCA if and when the contract actually comes into being. 

   

 ***** 

   

 49.   The type of case in which s. 542(1)(b) TCA does apply is canvassed in the course of the - sparse - case law addressing similar provisions in the United Kingdom . One example is suggested by the judgment of Buckley LJ in Eastham when he distinguished the case before him from a situation described by Jenkins LJ in Parway Estates Ltd. v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue (1958) 45 TC 135, 146: 

   

 'if one has a contract of sale and purchase which is expressed to be conditional on the happening of some event - the procuring of some consent or something of that sort - the contract for sale and purchase is in abeyance until such time as the condition is fulfilled ...' 

   

 50.   The judgment of Walton J. in Lyon gave another: 

   

 ' It would, for example, be possible for a hotelier to make a booking with a tour operator conditionally upon the next Olympic Games being held in London. Then, until it had been decided that the next Olympic Games were going to be held in London, there would be no effective contract: the whole contract would be conditional, the whole liabilities and duties between the parties would only arise when the condition was fulfilled.' 

   

 51.   Central to all of the cases is a critical distinction. There will, of course, be contracts in which the ability of one, other or both parties to perform the principal obligation they have assumed (here, the contract of sale) is dependent on certain events occurring or not occurring. It is open to those parties when framing their agreement to define the consequences where those events occur or do not occur. They can provide that the agreement is determined, and the obligations of the parties discharged, they can provide for substituted - or for that matter partial - performance, or they can stipulate that some or all of the obligations under the agreement will not arise if those events do not occur (or, as the case may be, do occur). They can also say that there is no contractual obligation of any kind to perform the principal obligation pending the event. If they say nothing about any of the foregoing, the law may imply appropriate provisions. But there remains a fundamental difference between a contract for sale which once existed and is determined, or may be repudiated, when the event does not occur as anticipated, and a case where there was never any such contract for sale at all. 

   

 52.   Differentiating a term that is a precondition to any obligation to transfer the asset from one that merely extinguishes or discharges an obligation to transfer that has come into being is, necessarily, an exercise that is heavily dependent on the construction of the agreement as a whole. It is a matter for the parties to agree whether a term has one effect or the other, and to express that agreement in their written contract. If it is the case that there is to be no contractual obligation to dispose of an asset unless and until certain licences and permissions are granted, one would expect that this would usually be clearly signalled in the agreement. Otherwise, the purchaser, in particular, could find themselves facing a legal liability to acquire an asset which, without the benefit of those licences, is worth considerably less to them that they paid for it. As it was put by Coulson J. in Persimmon Homes (South Coast) Ltd. v. Hall Aggregates (South Coast) Ltd., Cemex UK Properties Ltd. [2008] EWHC 2379 (TCC) at para. 298: 

   

 ' if one party's obligation to do something under a contract is contingent upon the happening of a particular event, the circumstances of that event must be identified unambiguously in the contract. It must be clear beyond doubt how and in what circumstances the relevant obligation has been triggered.' 

   

 53.   In characterising an agreement for this purpose, it is possible to identify some pointers. Obviously, the surest guide to the contracting parties' intentions is what they have actually and expressly provided for in the Agreement. That contracting parties who wish to render performance of the principal obligation conditional on an event will be generally expected to say this, seems a reliable starting point. If they have not, the agreement may still be characterised as conditional in this sense if the document as a whole placed in context makes it clear that that this was what was intended. In particular, if satisfaction of a condition is dependent on the actions of a contracting party it is more likely to be a condition the failure of which results in discharge or extinguishment of an existing obligation. If satisfaction is dependent on the actions of a third party, it is more likely to be a condition that prevents any obligation to sell from arising in the first place (see Nautica Marine Ltd. v. Trafigura Trading LLC (The 'Leonidas') [2020] EWHC 1986 (Comm) per Foxton J. at para. 49; [2021] 1 All ER 1157 (Comm)). But whether or not this is so depends on the context and wording of the agreement and all of the surrounding circumstances. For example, if the consent of a third party was pro forma and/or there were limited circumstances in which that consent could be lawfully withheld, the case for the condition precluding the creation of obligation to sell is considerably weaker. Moreover, in a situation in which an agreement does not clearly and expressly make the disposition conditional on identified events, other factors can be of critical importance. In particular, where a contract is entered into in a sector of the economy that is closely regulated, the terms of the governing legislative context may assume decisive importance in determining whether the agreement was - or could ever have been - conditional in this sense. 

   

 ***** 

   

 54.   Those distinctions and considerations I think, permit the formulation of a description of the circumstances in which s. 542(1)(b) TCA is properly engaged. The provision operates where, and only where, there is: 

   

 (a)    a legally enforceable contract between A and B; 

 (b)    ' under' which it might be said that A has agreed to dispose of, and B to acquire, an asset the disposition of which is subject to Capital Gains Tax; 

 (c)    where the obligation of A to dispose of, and that of B to acquire that asset is conditional upon an event; and, 

 (d)    where no contractual obligation to dispose of, and no obligation to acquire, that asset comes into being unless and until that event occurs. This is to be distinguished from the situation in which there is a contractual obligation to dispose of or acquire the asset irrespective of whether the 'event' occurs, but where the non-occurrence of the event may operate generally, or after the effluxion of a period of time, to extinguish that obligation, or to allow one or other parties to treat itself as discharged from any obligation of performance. 

   

 55.   Accordingly, the contract in issue here can only be properly described as ' conditional' if on its true construction the mutual obligations of the purchaser (to pay for and accept delivery of the vessel, the appurtenant equipment and its ' capacity' ) and of the appellant (to deliver same) were made by the contract contingent on the regulatory authorities allowing the transfer of tonnage, registering it as owner or granting an operative Sea Fishing Licence to the purchaser. For the following six reasons, the appellant has failed to establish that the Agreement was so contingent. 

   

 56.   First, the premise of the case was never made out. The Agreement did not refer to the grant of a sea-fishing licence, the registration of the vessel in the name of the purchaser, or the registration of specified tonnage and engine capacity. Instead, it referred to ' fishing entitlements' in terms that suggested that the confirmation of those rights was something that could be procured - if not provided - by the appellant himself and then tendered by him at completion. If what was intended was the collection of regulatory consents now contended for by the appellant - and putting aside the glib but hardly irrelevant observation that this could have been easily stated - it is very difficult to see how the Commissioner or a court could superimpose this on the written agreement without at least some evidence of context that would permit the conclusion that as a matter of trade practice, this was what the term meant and would have been objectively understood to mean by those conversant with the industry. This is particularly the case given that it was a matter for the purchaser to obtain the sea-fishing boat licence and ensure his registration. On this basis alone, it would appear to me that the appellant has failed to make out his case. 

   

 57.   Second, this was not the only evidential difficulty facing the appellant. At least in oral argument, he placed very substantial weight on his claim that the ' capacity' referred to in the Agreement referred to some form of fishing allocation, and that this had to be surrendered, extinguished and reissued by the authorities. In fact, the documentary evidence put before the Commissioner suggested that the capacity was simply assigned, and this was what the Agreement envisaged. Faced with this, if the appellant were to contend that an agreement was dependent upon actions of the regulatory authorities which were so uncertain that it was necessary for the parties to make the entire agreement contingent on the taking of those steps, it was a matter for him to lay contextual evidence before the Commissioner from which he could so conclude. The same, it should be stated, can be said of the question of obtaining a sea-fishing boat licence, or obtaining registration of the vessel after the transfer of ownership occurs. 

   

 58.   Third, the appellant faced a fundamental legal difficulty in advancing this case. The only way the sea-fishing boat licence and, thereafter, registration of the vessel could be obtained by the purchaser was if he first became owner of the vessel. On its face, this was not consistent with there being no contractual obligation to dispose of the vessel unless and until inter alia that licence and registration was obtained. The legislative context would suggest that the Agreement necessarily envisaged that transfer preceded the licence and registration. The initial response suggested by the appellant - that the execution of the Bill of Sale and accompanying declaration of ownership by the purchaser was in some sense a preliminary or procedural step necessitated by the applicable legal regime - was, to say the least, a deeply unattractive one. But, importantly, counsel accepted before this Court that by 22 December 2015 ownership of the vessel had transferred, adopting the position that the capacity had not. 

   

 59.   This points coercively to the conclusion that the agreement was one where, if the failure to obtain the sea-fishing boat licence or registration were to have any effect, it would discharge the agreement pursuant to which ownership of the vessel was transferred. Without at the very least a very clear mechanism in the Agreement itself enabling that transfer to be not merely unwound but wiped from the official record (if indeed such a mechanism could ever be devised) it could not plausibly be said that there was no contract for sale of any kind until that licence were issued. The features of the agreement relied upon by the appellant - the reference at clause 1.1 of the Agreement to the sale being ' subject to the provisions of this agreement' , the opaque reference to ' fishing entitlements' in Schedule 2 of the Agreement, and the fact that the purchaser had purchased capacity and that he could not have operated the vessel without registration and a sea-fishing boat licence - did not fill the gap arising from the omission of any such mechanism from the contract. 

   

 60.   Fourth, it is not true to say, either as a matter of general principle or as a matter of construction of s. 542(1) TCA, that (as the appellant contended) where the parties make provision for an event over which neither has control, the contract is for that reason alone conditional in the sense contended for by the appellant and, therefore, that there is no contractual obligation to transfer the asset unless and until that event occurs. No authority was cited in support of that proposition. Parties must be - and are - entirely free to enter into legally binding contractual arrangements on the assumption that an uncertain event outside their control will occur, or for that matter that the non-occurrence of that event would not prevent some obligations from arising between them. That a contract may be affected by such an event within the contemplation of the parties may, where the event is genuinely outside their control, weigh towards the agreement being conditional in the sense that there was no binding obligation at all to undertake particular performance. But it remains only one relevant factor in the exercise of characterisation. 

   

 61.   Fifth, and conversely, nor is it correct to propose (as the appellant did) that the doctrine of frustration does not apply where an event that has been contemplated by the parties occurs: ' [i]t is by no means necessary to prove that the event in question was not foreseen by the parties because frustration is a flexible enough doctrine to apply in a proper case' (Clarke, Contract Law in Ireland (9 th edn., Round Hall 2022) at para. [18-94]) citing Ocean Trump Tankers Corp. v. V/O Sovfracht (The Eugenia) [1964] 1 All ER 161 and the High Court decision in Neville and Sons Ltd. v. Guardian Builders Ltd. [1995] 1 ILRM 1 (overturned on other grounds by this court). Certainly, it may be more difficult to make a case in frustration where the event was foreseeable and foreseen, it being less likely that the doctrine will be precluded where the event is foreseeable but not foreseen (see Chitty, at para. [27.090]). What is critical and usually dispositive, is whether the parties have made provision in their contract for the event: if they have, it will not be open to them to assert that the event has in fact frustrated the contract. But where, as here, no such provision has been made, there is nothing in principle that prevents the doctrine of frustration from operating. 

   

 62.   Finally, the proposition urged by the appellant that a term should be implied into the Agreement in order to give it ' business efficacy' is misconceived. This court has in a sequence of cases - Tradax (Ireland) Ltd. v. Irish Grain Board [1984] IR 1, Sweeney v. Duggan [1997] 2 IR 531, Carna Foods Ltd. v. Eagle Star Insurance Company (Ireland) Ltd. [1997] 2 IR 193, Dakota Packaging Ltd. v. AGP Manufacturing BV t/a Wyeth Medica Ireland [2005] 2 IR 54 and HSE v. O'Sullivan [2023] IESC 11 - described exhaustively the conditions under which terms will be implied into a written agreement. All of the cases make it clear that a term will be implied only where it is necessary, not where it is reasonable or seems, with the benefit of hindsight, sensible. They also make it clear that the term to be implied must be capable of precise expression. 

   

 63.   Whatever about the necessity for terms that would enable the purchaser to extricate themselves from some or all of the obligations imposed by the provisions of the Agreement in the event that those consents and permissions were not forthcoming, there is no basis on which it can be said that it is ' necessary' that the law deem a contract for the sale of the vessel to have never existed. The only reason this is said to be now ' necessary' is that the vendor wishes to avail of a tax advantage that will accrue if the Agreement is construed as being subject to such a condition. That is not a consideration that gives rise to ' business efficacy' . At most, it gives rise to a fiscal benefit for one party to the Agreement. That is not a commercial necessity, but a financial advantage. 

   

 64.   This is aside from the framing of the term contended for by the appellant - ' [i]f the purchaser is not granted fishing entitlements due to the exercise of its discretion or the Licensing Authority, the purchaser will not be liable to the vendor for the purchase monies and will take such steps as are necessary to reverse any steps which have been taken with regard to the registration of ownership of the vessel' . This is not precise, but general and convoluted. It is exactly the kind of cumbersome provision that a court will never imply. It is, to revert to a more fundamental point made earlier, one that shows that the Agreement could only have functioned if it had some legal effect before the event which, it is now contended, prevented it from having any such effect. 

   

   

 ***** 

   

   

 65.   In these circumstances, this appeal should be dismissed, and - save in two respects - the questions framed by the Commissioner in the case stated should be answered as proposed by the High Court and Court of Appeal. The first exception is Question 2: it asks ' Did the Commissioner err in paragraph 38.5 of his Determination in stating that one of the steps required to be taken under the Memorandum of Agreement was to 'ensure licence and fishing rights were transferred to the purchaser' rather than 'be surrendered by the vendor and the purchaser given equivalent fishing rights'? If so, does this have any impact on the Memorandum being conditional in nature? The court was not provided with an evidential basis on which the first part of this question should be answered, although the second part was correctly responded to in the negative. The second is Question 4, where the Commissioner inquired as to whether he was correct in contending that if the procedural steps were not fulfilled, the Memorandum would have been frustrated. It is not necessary to determine if this is so, and the answer should be that the Memorandum would have been either frustrated, or otherwise discharged and/or the contracting parties would have been entitled to rescind and/or repudiate same. The question of which of these was the appropriate remedy would depend on the circumstances in which the procedural steps were not fulfilled.
